article_text:
The red carpet at the Academy Museum Gala is now open.

Once again, the event is proving to be one of Hollywood’s most glamorous A-list nights of the year.

Among those expected to walk the carpet are Taylor Swift, Connor Storrie, Jessica Biel and Justin Timberlake, Kim Kardashian, Jacob Elordi, Kendall Jenner, Eva Longoria, Salma Hayek, Inde Navarrette, Nia Long, McKenna Grace, Rosé, Sabrina Carpenter, Drew Starkey, Janelle Monáe, Pamela Anderson, Charles Melton, Alexander Skarsgård, Tom Ford and many others.

The program for the sixth annual gala, which takes place at and benefits the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures, includes honoring Charlize Theron with the Icon Award, Colman Domingo with the Vantage Award and John Carpenter with the Luminary Award.

Not only did Taylor Swift perform during the evening, but the gala raised more than $14 million.

The gala, presented by Rolex, is co-chaired by Robert Rodriguez, Steven Spielberg and Kate Capshaw and Tom Ford.

The host committee includes Jessica Alba, Judd Apatow and Leslie Mann, Autumn Durald Arkapaw, Adrien Brody and Georgina Chapman, Jon M. Chu, Kirsten Dunst, Nicholas Galitzine, Ludwig and Serena Göransson, Regina Hall, Kate Hudson, Jessica Lange, Greta Lee, John Legend and Chrissy Teigen, Rami Malek, Demi Moore, Olivia Munn, Gina Prince-Bythewood, Questlove, Da’Vine Joy Randolph, Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen, Bird Runningwater and Teyana Taylor.

Check out photos of all the red carpet arrivals below.

article_text:
アンリ・マティスの展覧会「マティス 黒と白の詩学—ピエール＆タナ・マティス財団の版画コレクションを中心に」が、2027年3月20日〜7月19日に東京・上野の 国立西洋美術館 で開催される。

20世紀を代表するフランスの画家、アンリ・マティス（1869〜1954）。フォーヴィスム（野獣派）のリーダー的存在として知られ、鮮烈な色彩と卓越した線描による独自の表現を追求した。その革新的な造形は、近代美術に大きな影響を与え、現代に至るまで多くの人々を魅了し続けている。

マティスは、生涯を通じて版画や挿絵本の制作にも取り組み、木版やモノタイプから、リトグラフ、エッチング、リノカット、アクアティントまで、幅広い技法によって800点以上の版画や多数の挿絵本を残した。マティスにとっては、絵画、素描、彫刻、切り絵、版画はいずれも等しく重要な自己表現の手段であり、ジャンルやメディアを自由に横断しながら様々な試みを続けた。

ニューヨークのピエール＆タナ・マティス財団の特別協力のもとで行われる本展では、同財団の版画コレクションを核に、関連する絵画やデッサン類もあわせて展示。初期から晩年までのマティスの版画制作の歩みをたどりながら、その意味と意義を考察する。

マティスは、同時代の多くの芸術家と異なり、版画制作においていくつかの例外を除いて、黒と白の表現に徹した。展覧会では、「黒と白」というテーマのもと、マティスの版画・挿絵本の意義と魅力に新たな光を当てることを目指し、版画とともに絵画や素描を比較展示することで、マティス芸術全体の根幹に関わる線と空間の関係性や色彩に対する考察を掘り下げていく。

あわせて、希少な原版の展示や刷られた紙の種類の比較などを通じ、マティスの版画制作プロセスの直接的な理解も目指す。また、マティス芸術における挿絵本の重要性に注目することも展覧会の特徴のひとつになっている。

本展は、マティスのエッセンスが凝縮された版画と挿絵本の展示から、様々な版画技法で奏でた「黒と白」の多彩な響きと、豊かな創造の世界に触れられる貴重な機会となりそうだ。

「マティス 黒と白の詩学—ピエール＆タナ・マティス財団の版画コレクションを中心に」

editorial_excerpt_zh: “永恒而脆弱的显现”（Eterne e fragili presenze）是带Bertozzi & Casoni作品走进米兰巴加蒂·瓦尔塞基博物馆（Museo Bagatti Valsecchi）的展览。该项目汇集了约30件作品，其中10件专为这座故居博物馆的空间构思，将物质的持久性与不稳定性联系在一起……

Bertozzi）和斯特凡诺·达尔·蒙蒂·卡索尼（Stefano Dal Monte Casoni，1961–2023）于1980年在伊莫拉创立，他们将陶瓷转化为一种颠覆性工具，打破了珍贵与废弃、自然与人工、高雅文化与大众想象之间的等级秩序。在卡索尼去世后，贝尔托齐以两人的共同名字继续创作，为持久性这一主题赋予了更深的回响。作品在其起源条件发生变化的同时依然存在。", "links": article_text:
La ceramica non cristallizza il simbolo: lo imbalsama. Nel lavoro di Bertozzi & Casoni , la materia trattiene l’apparenza del reale quando la vita sembra essersi già ritirata. Sottratta al divenire, la forma acquista una nuova e ambigua esistenza, sospesa tra permanenza e perdita. È questa tensione a orientare la mostra. Fondato a Imola nel 1980 da Giampaolo Bertozzi e Stefano Dal Monte Casoni (1961–2023), il sodalizio ha trasformato la ceramica in uno strumento di sovversione delle gerarchie tra prezioso e scarto, natura e artificio, cultura alta e immaginario popolare. Dopo la scomparsa di Casoni, Bertozzi prosegue sotto il nome condiviso, conferendo ulteriore risonanza al tema della persistenza. L’opera continua a esistere mentre mutano le condizioni della sua origine.

La cornice del Museo Bagatti Valsecchi , che ospita fino al 25 ottobre 2026 la mostra Eterne e fragili presenze , a cura di Alberto Mattia Martini in collaborazione con Galleria Giovanni Bonelli, intensifica questa riflessione. Gli oggetti storici della casa-museo custodiscono le tracce di un mondo; le sculture di Bertozzi & Casoni ne ricostruiscono l’apparenza attraverso una materia durevole, capace di simulare il vivente. La conservazione come testimonianza incontra così la conservazione come artificio. In questo confronto, il passato diventa una misura attraverso cui interrogare l’autenticità delle presenze contemporanee. In Enigma (2026), un naso sproporzionato, di ascendenza pinocchiesca, perfora libri d’arte. La menzogna irrompe nel luogo deputato alla trasmissione del sapere e alla legittimazione culturale. Il gesto, ironico e destabilizzante, incrina la fiducia nella rappresentazione: quanto di ciò che riconosciamo come vero è già costruzione, convenzione, artificio? Il naso diventa così una figura dell’ambiguità delle immagini e dell’autorità che attribuiamo loro.

Con Cuccia Brillo con setter inglese (2018), l’immaginario del consumo incontra la rappresentazione animale. La cuccia e il setter evocano una domesticità riconoscibile, che la traduzione ceramica sottrae alla quotidianità e consegna a una presenza sospesa. Il riferimento pop rivela quanto il rapporto con gli oggetti e gli animali sia mediato da immagini, desideri e modelli culturali. La verosimiglianza seduce e, insieme, lascia emergere la natura artificiale della scena. In Dove Come Quando (2014), opera in ceramica policroma, i fiori crescono sulle corna di un cerbiatto. La materia dà forma a una metamorfosi: ciò che appartiene alla crescita e alla difesa dell’animale diventa luogo di fioritura. Il corpo si apre a una vitalità vegetale che ne trasfigura la presenza, intrecciando delicatezza e perturbazione, fissità e rigenerazione.

La ceramica trattiene l’immagine di una natura in trasformazione: la forma resta immobile, mentre la fioritura evoca un processo vitale. Nella Grottesca , il volto di una scimmia compare su piatti, introducendo una presenza animale in un oggetto legato alla domesticità e al rituale quotidiano. Il supporto, associato alla funzione e alla consuetudine, diventa superficie d’apparizione. Il titolo richiama una tradizione in cui il grottesco altera i confini tra umano e animale, ordine e deformazione. È il cortocircuito tra immagine e oggetto d’uso a incrinare la familiarità del quotidiano. La ricerca di Bertozzi & Casoni eccede la celebrazione dell’iperrealismo.

Il confronto con Duane Hanson o Ron Mueck aiuta a inquadrare la capacità della scultura di generare una presenza quasi tangibile; nel lavoro del duo, tuttavia, la precisione mimetica apre una questione ulteriore: ciò che sembra vivo è già sottratto alla vita. Il simulacro assume così una consistenza autonoma: riproduce i tratti del reale senza restituirne l’esperienza. La riflessione di Jean Baudrillard offre una chiave di lettura per questa instabilità, in cui vero e falso restano in tensione. Anche il pensiero di Walter Benjamin sull’autenticità e sull’irripetibile «qui e ora» dell’opera risuona in tale scarto. La ceramica permane, mentre l’istante vivente da cui l’immagine sembra provenire resta irrecuperabile.

Il titolo Eterne e fragili presenze condensa il paradosso della mostra: la materia resiste, mentre la vita resta inafferrabile. Nel cerbiatto fiorito di Dove Come Quando , la fissità accoglie persino l’idea di una rigenerazione possibile. Le opere si muovono tra la durata dell’oggetto e la precarietà del vivente, facendo della loro tensione il centro dell’esperienza. Mentre Bertozzi & Casoni fabbricano l’immagine del tempo che passa, la ceramica conserva ciò che non può più accadere. Davanti alle loro opere, il reale si avvicina fino a diventare tangibile, e proprio allora rivela la distanza incolmabile dalla vita.

article_text:
Neon has joined The Guardian, MK2, James Wilson and Jonathan Glazer on explosive doc NAZA from Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the co-directors of No Other Land .

The film was released independently in the U.S. on September 30 in 85 theaters across 30 cities. Overseas, the film has secured theatrical distribution in more than 50 countries. Neon will now work with the filmmakers to expand its footprint and to “reach larger audiences and communities”.

The deal was negotiated by MK2 Films, who boarded the film for sales prior to the Venice film festival, and Neon.

Related Stories

Israeli Cinema Professionals Talk Hopes & Fears Ahead Of Knife-Edge Election: "It's Like A Horror Film Because I Don't Know What Is Behind The Door"

'NAZA' Tops $1 Million With Neon, Solid Limited Expansion For 'La Bola Negra' -- Specialty Box Office

The Venice Film Festival debut charts secret conversations on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night which “reveal the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza by the people who designed and operated them.”

Watch on Deadline

Neon stated: “Yuval and Rachel have created one of the best films of the year; it’s an extraordinary work of art and eyewitness testimony that stands alongside landmark documentaries like Laura Poitras’ Citizenfour and Joshua Oppenheimer’s The Act Of Killing . At the heart of Neon’s mission is a commitment to championing the best cinema from around the world. We’re proud to join the incredible team already working on the film and help bring it to the widest audience possible.”

The documentary received its world premiere in competition at the Venice International Film Festival where it won the Special Jury Prize and received a record-breaking twenty-five-minute standing ovation. The film later screened at the San Sebastián International Film Festival (winning the audience award) and New York Film Festival. This week, it won the Critics Prize at the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival. The film is nominated for three Critics Choice Documentary Awards including Best Documentary, Best Director(s) and Best Political Documentary. It is also included on DOC NYC’s Short List.

The documentary is produced by The Guardian with producer James Wilson’s JW Films in association with Placeholder Films and Unseen Hand. Jonathan Glazer ( The Zone of Interest ) executive-produced.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Cinema Guild has acquired North American distribution rights for German Angela Schanelec ’s My Wife Cries (Meine Frau weint) , written and directed by Angela Schanelec.

The film premiered inCompetition at the 76th Berlin International Film Festival ealier this year and recently played in the Main Slate selection of the 64th New York Film Festival.

The study of the dynamics of a Berlin couple, the film opens with Thomas (Vladimir Vulevic), a crane operator, awaiting a call from his wife, Carla (Agathe Bonitzer), a nursery-school teacher.

Related Stories

'The Ballad of Suzanne Césaire' Begins Theatrical Run Today In NYC, Filmmaker Madeleine Hunt-Ehrlich Breaks Down How She Crafted The Buzzy Feature -- The Deadline Q&A

Cinema Guild Acquires Restored Films Of French New Wave Master Luc Moullet

But she is curled up on a bench outside a hospital, bereft over the death of another man, her dance class partner. Thomas finds her and sits beside her until she is ready to return home; the walk there reveals a secret that opens a rift of no return.

Watch on Deadline

Written and directed by Schanelec, My Wife Cries follows her experiemental works I Was at Home, But… (2019) and Music (2023).

“Schanelec finds extraordinary emotional depth in the smallest exchanges between people,” said Cinema Guild President Peter Kelly. “We’re proud to continue bringing her films to North American audiences with this moving and surprising work.”

The deal was negotiated by Peter Kelly and Dylan Foley of Cinema Guild and Kevin Chneiweiss of Paris-based SBS.

Vulevic and Bonitzer are joined by Birte Schnöink, and Pauline Rebmann in the cast, with cinematography by Marius Panduru and editing by Schanelec.

The film is produced by Kirill Krasovski for Blue Monticola Film, in co-production with SBS Productions, Maier Bros., and Unitbase.

Schanelec previously received the Berlinale’s Silver Bear for Best Director for I Was at Home, But… and the Silver Bear for Best Screenplay for Music .

Cinema Guild’s further upcoming releases include Hong Sangsoo’s The Day She Returns, Nowhere to Lay My Eyes and Ted Fendt’s Foreign Travel.

Recent releases include Otar Iosseliani’s restorations, Kamal Aljafari’s With Hasan in Gaza , Hong Sangsoo’s What Does That Nature Say to You , and Aleksandre Koberidze’s Dry Leaf .

article_text:
Oscar-winning prosthetic makeup artist Kazu Hiro has been in the industry for over 30 years. He’s transformed Bradley Cooper, Gary Oldman, Charlize Theron and, most recently, Dwayne Johnson in “The Smashing Machine.”

This year, he was tasked with transforming Tom Cruise in “ Digger ,” in which Cruise plays a Texas oil tycoon. But this isn’t the Cruise audiences are typically familiar with — the dashing Hollywood movie star who jumps off cliffs and hangs off airplane wings. No, Digger is an aged man with jowls, thinning hair, a disheveled appearance and a belly.

Related Stories

‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on AI: 'An Amazing Piece of Technology’ but ‘I’m Not Embracing It at All’

The film is directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu and also stars Riz Ahmed, John Goodman and Sandra Hüller and follows Digger, whose company causes a potential global catastrophe.

That transformation could have taken hours — six to be precise. Except Cruise didn’t want to spend that long in the makeup chair putting prosthetics on. He was convinced the team could do it faster, and Hiro did. He pulled it off, finding a way to streamline the process.

Hiro spoke with Variety about his process and how he transformed Cruise into the oil baron.

My agent called me and said Alejandro wanted to talk to me about this project. I wanted to read the script before I met him, and I read it and it was amazing, with a great story.

We had a conversation, but he’s supposed to be an oil tycoon. At that time, he was around 76 years old, much older than the final look.

I went to see Tom in London, and we had a meeting with him and Alejandro — it was an open idea at the time. He was on a tight schedule because he was shooting “Mission Impossible,” but we set up time to do a 3D scan, live caps and photographs and I started to sculpt. Alejandro liked the first design.

As I was about to finish the sculpture and started to make a mold of each piece, he called and said, “Digger should be 67 years old.” So, I took another look and finished that in a few weeks. But I also made a third design, and the final look was a mix of those.

It was full coverage — 12 pieces. The test makeup took less than five hours. The second day went down to two and a half, which is a good time for prosthetics makeup. But Tom wanted to be in makeup during rehearsals, which was six weeks before filming and we had to do it.

Tom has spoken about this, but said, “I had a guy there with a stopwatch and I’m like, ‘OK, you see that time, six hours? By the time we’re done, we’re going to get it under an hour,’” When Tom Cruise says that, you do it.

Two hours and 15 minutes is a good time, including hair work and putting on a wig. I can just slap on prosthetics and paint and put the wig on in one hour, but it will sacrifice the quality. To do good work, you need to spend time on each process to maintain the quality every day. I always try not to spend too much in the chair because I understand the actor has to work afterward, and the hours in the day are limited. And so I always try to figure it out.

What I usually do is I have an assistant right next to me write down how long it took. If I feel OK, this may be faster or this may be longer than the day before, I ask, “OK, how long was it?” And I adjust my timing for the other applications. I don’t want to delay the whole process of filming, and I always try to finish on time or shorter. It has to be done as he requested.

Yes, he did. We made a prosthetic version for the beginning of the film when he’s not wearing a shirt.

But under the suits, we made spandex and glued down prosthetics on it because he didn’t want to glue it (the prosthetic belly) on him. I said, “Are you sure? This is going to be heavy and hard to wear?” He said, “Yes, I’m trained and can handle it. So he started to wear that.”

There was a bald cap and, under bald cap, forehead, cheek, nose. The neck and chin were attached. And there were wig and eyebrow pieces. In the end, it was seven.

I cannot …(laughs).
